source_text: τὰ δ’ ἑξῆς προςαποδοτέον καὶ τὴν ἐκ τῆς βαρβάρου φιλοσοφίας Ελληνικὴν κλοπὴν σαφέστερον ἤδη παραστατέον. Φασὶ γὰρ σῶμα εἶναι τὸν θεὸν οἱ Στωϊκοὶ καὶ πνεῦμα κατ’ οὐσίαν, ὥσπερ ἀμέλει καὶ τὴν ψυχήν. πάντα ταῦτα ἄντικρυς εὑρήσεις ἐν ταῖς γραφαῖς. μὴ γάρ μοι τὰς ἀλληγορίας αὐτῶν ἐννοήσῃς τὰ νῦν ὡς ἡ γνωστικὴ παραδίδωσιν ἀλήθεια, εἰ ἄλλο τι δεικνύουσαι, καθάπερ οἱ σοφοὶ παλαισταί, ἄλλο μηνύουσιν. ἀλλ’ οἳ μὲν διήκειν διὰ πάσης τῆς οὐσίας τὸν θεόν φασιν, ἡμεῖς δὲ ποιητὴν μόνον αὐτὸν καλοῦμεν καὶ λόγῳ ποιητήν. παρήγαγεν δὲ αὐτοὺς τὸ ἐν τῇ Σοφίᾳ εἰρημένον διήκει δὲ καὶ χωρεῖ διὰ πάντων διὰ τὴν καθαριότητα, ἐπεὶ μὴ συνῆκαν λέγεσθαι ταῦτα ἐπὶ τῆς σοφίας τῆς πρωτοκτίστου τῷ θεῷ. ναί, φασίν, ἀλλὰ ὕλην ὑποτίθενται οἱ φιλόσοφοι ἐν ταῖς ἀρχαῖς, οἵ τε Στωϊκοὶ καὶ Πλάτων καὶ Πυθαγόρας, ἀλλὰ καὶ Ἀριστοτέλης ὁ Περιπατητικός, οὐχὶ δὲ μίαν ἀρχήν. ἴστωσαν οὖν τὴν καλουμένην ὕλην ἄποιον καὶ ἀσχημάτιστον λεγομένην πρὸς αὐτῶν, καὶ τολμηρότερον ἤδη μὴ ὂν πρὸς τοῦ Πλάτωνος εἰρῆσθαι. καὶ μή τι μυστικώτατα μίαν τὴν ὄντως οὖσαν ἀρχὴν εἰδὼς ἐν τῷ Τιμαίῳ αὐταῖς φησι λέξεσιν· νῦν δ’ οὖν τὸ παρ’ ἡμῶν ὧδε ἐχέτω· τὴν μὲν περὶ πάντων εἴτε ἀρχὴν εἴτε ἀρχὰς εἴτε ὅπῃ δοκεῖ τούτων πέρι, τὸ νῦν οὐ ῥητέον, δἰ ἄλλο μὲν οὐδέν, διὰ δὲ τὸ χαλεπὸν εἶναι κατὰ τὸν παρόντα τρόπον τῆς διεξόδου δηλῶσαι τὰ δοκοῦντα. ἄλλως τε ἡ λέξις ἡ προφητικὴ ἐκείνη ἡ δὲ γῆ ἦν ἀόρατος καὶ ἀκατασκεύαστος ἀφορμὰς αὐτοῖς ὑλικῆς οὐσίας παρέσχηται. Ναὶ μὴν Ἐπικούρῳ μὲν ἡ τοῦ αὐτομάτου παρείσδυσις οὐ παρακολουθήσαντι τῷ ῥητῷ γέγονεν ἐντεῦθεν ματαιότης ματαιοτήτων, τὰ πάντα ματαιότης. Ἀριστοτέλει δὲ μέχρι σελήνης ἐπῆλθε καταγαγεῖν τὴν πρόνοιαν ἐκ τοῦδε τοῦ ψαλμοῦ· κύριε, ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ τὸ ἔλεός σου καὶ ἡ ἀλήθειά σου ἕως τῶν νεφελῶν. οὐδέπω γὰρ ἀποκεκάλυπτο ἡ τῶν προφητικῶν δήλωσις μυστηρίων πρὸ τῆς τοῦ κυρίου παρουσίας. Τάς τε αὖ μετὰ θάνατον κολάσεις καὶ τὴν διὰ πυρὸς τιμωρίαν ἀπὸ τῆς βαρβάρου φιλοσοφίας ἥ τε ποιητικὴ πᾶσα μοῦσα, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἡ Ἑλληνικὴ φιλοσοφία ὑφείλετο.
thought_title: Greek Philosophy's Debt to Barbarian Wisdom
pass_a_gloss: But the next things must be given back and the Greek theft from barbarian philosophy must be shown more clearly. For the Stoics say that God is a body and spirit in essence, just as also the soul. You will find all these things stated plainly in the scriptures. Do not think about their allegories now as the gnosis delivers the truth, if they show something else, just as the ancient wise men show something else. But they say that God permeates every essence, we however call Him only the Creator and the Creator by word. The statement in Wisdom led them astray, 'He permeates and extends through all things because of purity', since they did not understand that these things are said about the primal wisdom of God. Yes, they say, but the philosophers hypothesize matter in the beginnings, both the Stoics and Plato and Pythagoras, and also Aristotle the Peripatetic, not one principle. Let them know therefore the so-called matter, uncreated and unformed, as it is said by them, and more boldly not said by Plato. And knowing the one truly existing principle, he says in the Timaeus with the same words. Now therefore let our position be this: the thing about all things, whether principle or principles or however it seems, is not to be said now, because of nothing else, but because it is difficult to show the opinions in the present manner of exposition. Besides, the prophetic speech, 'the earth was invisible and unformed', gave them opportunities for material substance. For Epicurus, the idea of the automatic did not follow from what was said, and thus came about the vanity of vanities, all things are vanity. And Aristotle drew down providence to the moon from this psalm, 'Lord, your mercy and truth extend to the clouds'. For the explanation of prophetic mysteries had not yet been revealed before the Lord's presence. And the punishments after death and the punishment by fire, and all the poetic Muses, but also Greek philosophy, were derived from barbarian philosophy.

pass_b_english: The next step is to return what is owed and to expose more clearly the Greek appropriation of barbarian philosophy. The Stoics declare that God is a body and spirit in essence, just as they regard the soul. You will find all these points stated plainly in the scriptures. Do not mistake their allegories for the truth that the gnosis now delivers; if they indicate something else, they do so in the way ancient sages hint at one thing while meaning another. The Stoics claim that God permeates every essence, but we call Him only the Creator — the Creator by His Word. They were led astray by the saying in Wisdom: "He permeates and extends through all things because of purity," since they did not understand that these words refer to the primal Wisdom created by God. "Yes," they object, "but the philosophers posit matter among the first principles — Stoics, Plato, Pythagoras, and even Aristotle the Peripatetic — not a single principle." Let them recognize, then, that this so-called matter is described by them as unqualified and unformed, and that Plato goes even further and says it does not exist. And in the Timaeus, knowing the one truly existing principle, he speaks of it in those very words. For now, let our position stand thus: whether there is one first principle or many, or whatever one supposes about them, we must not discuss it now — not for any other reason than that it is difficult to set forth the apparent truths in our present mode of exposition. Besides, the prophetic word, "the earth was invisible and unformed" (Genesis 1:2), supplied them with the raw material for a doctrine of material substance. Epicurus, failing to follow the text, slipped in the notion of the automatic and so arrived at "vanity of vanities, all is vanity." Aristotle, drawing from the psalm, "Lord, your mercy is in the heavens, and your truth reaches to the clouds" (Psalm 36:5), brought providence down only as far as the moon. For the revelation of the prophetic mysteries had not yet been unveiled before the Lord's coming. And the punishments after death, the punishment by fire, the whole poetic tradition of the Muses, and indeed Greek philosophy itself, all drew their origin from barbarian philosophy.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Greek text. Pass B correctly identifies and adds the required scripture citations for the Genesis and Psalm quotations which were present in the Greek text but lacked verse numbers. Pass A is a faithful gloss. The distinction regarding Plato's 'not being' (μὴ ὄν) is handled correctly in Pass B. All clauses, including the complex discussion on matter and the Stoic/Platonic/Aristotelian principles, are preserved.
